intro.html: Most of these words describe people who think too much of themselves, each in a different style: the arrogant person acts superior, the haughty one is cold and lofty, the condescending one talks down, the pompous one puffs up, the imperious one gives orders, and the supercilious one raises an eyebrow in scorn. Hubris is the kind of pride that leads to a fall.
On the other side stand three words of praise: modest, unassuming and self-effacing people don’t boast, don’t show off and don’t push themselves forward.

words.def: acting as if you are more important than others
words.ex: The {arrogant} new player refused to pass the ball to anyone.
words.ctx: He was talented, but his {arrogant} habit of interrupting everyone and dismissing their ideas soon left him with no partners for the project.
words.etym: From Latin arrogare, “to claim for oneself”: ad (to) + rogare (to ask).

mn.cue: AIR-OGANT: nose high in the AIR
mn.text: Victor struts down the street with his nose so high in the air that he never sees the people saying hello. He is {arrogant}.

scene.alt: A man in a top hat walks with his nose in the air, ignoring a boy who waves hello.

words.def: proud in a cold way that looks down on others
words.ex: The {haughty} duchess would not even glance at the servants.
words.ctx: Her {haughty} reply, delivered with a cool stare and a turned shoulder, made it clear that she thought the question beneath her.
words.etym: From haught, “high, proud,” from Old French haut (high), from Latin altus (high).

mn.text: Lady Greta stands on a box so she can look down on everyone, and she will not speak to anyone below her. She is {haughty}.

scene.alt: A haughty lady stands on a crate with her arms crossed, ignoring a girl who offers her a flower.

words.def: talking down to others as if they were less smart or important
words.ex: The salesman used a {condescending} tone, explaining what a “button” was.
words.ctx: Grandma has driven a tractor for fifty years, so she laughed at the young mechanic’s {condescending} lecture on how to start an engine.
words.etym: From Latin condescendere, “to stoop, come down”: con (with) + descendere (to come down).

mn.text: Rex bends way down to talk to the head chef as if she were a baby: “This is a SPOON.” His tone is {condescending}.

scene.alt: A man bends down to explain a spoon to an annoyed head chef.

words.def: self-important and showy in speech or manner
words.ex: The {pompous} duke gave a twenty-minute speech about himself at the ribbon cutting.
words.ctx: Instead of simply saying the bus was late, the {pompous} official announced that “transit services are experiencing a temporary scheduling irregularity.”
words.etym: From Late Latin pomposus, from pompa, “a procession, a grand display.”

mn.text: The duke arrives with a drumroll, a velvet cape and a speech all about how wonderful he is. He is {pompous}.

scene.alt: A duke in a cape and medals reads a long speech about himself while children yawn.

words.def: commanding and bossy, expecting to be obeyed
words.ex: With an {imperious} wave, the toddler sent his father back for more juice.
words.ctx: The new manager’s {imperious} style, barking orders and never asking for opinions, made the staff nostalgic for her gentle predecessor.
words.etym: From Latin imperiosus, “commanding,” from imperium (command, empire).

mn.text: From his high chair, little Theo points like an emperor: “Juice! Now!” And Dad runs to obey. Theo is {imperious}.

scene.alt: A toddler in a paper crown points and demands juice while his father rushes to bring it.

words.def: scornfully superior; looking down your nose at others
words.ex: The {supercilious} waiter raised an eyebrow at Pip’s muddy sneakers.
words.ctx: The critic’s review was {supercilious}: rather than discuss the play, he sneered at the small theater, its folding chairs and its “charmingly amateur” actors.
words.etym: From Latin supercilium, “eyebrow” (super, above + cilium, eyelid): the raised eyebrow of scorn.
words.note: It comes from the Latin word for eyebrow, not from “silly.”

mn.text: The snooty waiter raises one eyebrow at Pip’s muddy sneakers: “Hmm. Are you lost?” His look is {supercilious}.

scene.alt: A snobbish waiter looks down his nose at a boy in muddy sneakers.

words.def: too much pride, the kind that leads to a downfall
words.ex: In the old myths, a hero’s {hubris} usually ends in disaster.
words.ctx: The champion’s {hubris} cost him the title; sure that no one could beat him, he skipped training for a month and lost to an unknown in the first round.
words.etym: From Greek hybris, “insolence, excessive pride”; in Greek tragedy, such pride often brings a hero down.
words.note: Hubris is more than pride: it is pride that leads to a fall.

mn.cue: a HUGE BRAG before a fall
mn.text: “No wave can beat my castle!” Rex brags, building right at the water’s edge. The very next wave flattens it. His {hubris} brought him down.

labels.text: HU-BRAG-is: a HUGE BRAG, then a fall

scene.alt: A boastful man’s sandcastle is about to be swept away by a big wave.

words.def: not boasting about your abilities or achievements
words.ex: Though she had won the state prize, Kai’s sister was too {modest} to mention it.
words.ctx: The scientist was {modest} about her discovery; in every interview she praised her students and called herself “just the one who wrote it down.”
words.etym: From Latin modestus, “keeping due measure, moderate,” from modus (measure).
words.note: Modest can also mean not large: a modest house, a modest salary.

mn.cue: MOD-EST: never says he’s the BEST
mn.text: Kai wins first prize at the science fair but just says, “My friends helped a lot.” He never calls himself the best. He is {modest}.

scene.alt: A boy holding a trophy shrugs shyly and gives credit to his friends while a girl claps.

words.def: not drawing attention to yourself; quiet and humble
words.ex: The {unassuming} man in the back row turned out to be the famous author.
words.ctx: For a shop that sells the best bread in the state, it is surprisingly {unassuming}: no sign, no fancy windows, just a plain green door and a line of customers.

mn.text: The quiet woman in the plain sweater, reading in the back row, is the famous author everyone came to see. You’d never assume it: she is {unassuming}.

scene.alt: A plainly dressed woman reads quietly while a man looks around for the visiting author, not realizing it is her.

words.def: keeping yourself in the background; humble
words.ex: The {self-effacing} coach gave all the credit to her players.
words.ctx: Although he had built most of the robot himself, the {self-effacing} engineer stood at the back of the photo and told reporters that the team deserved the praise.
words.etym: From efface, “to rub out,” from French effacer: ex (out) + face (face, surface).

mn.text: When the team photo is taken, the coach steps to the very edge, nearly out of the picture, and says, “It was all them.” She is {self-effacing}.

scene.alt: Two teens cheer with a trophy while their coach stands far off at the edge of the picture.

head: word
the special flavor of pride
rows: talks down, as to a child
pride that leads to a fall
after.cap: Seven shades of too much pride.

after.html: Modest, unassuming and self-effacing all praise humility. Self-effacing is the strongest: such a person actively steps out of the spotlight.

choices: A sailor ignores every storm warning, sure that no sea can sink him, and his ship goes down.
A shy student wins a prize and thanks her teacher.
A cook spills soup and cleans it up.
A runner trains hard and wins a medal.
items.why: Hubris is pride so great that it leads to a fall: the sailor’s overconfidence sinks him.

items.q: True or false: supercilious comes from the word “silly.”
items.why: False. It comes from Latin supercilium, “eyebrow”: the raised eyebrow of a scornful person.

items.q: Which word best describes someone who gives orders and expects to be obeyed at once?
items.why: Imperious, from Latin imperium (command), means commanding and bossy.

items.q: True or false: a modest champion brags about every win.
items.why: False. A modest person does not boast.
